05 — Design Process · Fexle Services

Nimi — Group Travel Management App

Product Designer · 12–14 months
RoleProduct Designer
ClientFexle Services
Timeline12–14 months
TeamPM, team lead, 3 devs, QA, lead designer
Background

Three apps for one trip.

Group travel involves tracking shared expenses, managing logistics, and capturing shared memories. Most travellers handle these across separate tools — messaging apps for coordination, expense trackers for budgeting, social platforms for photos.

That fragmentation creates unnecessary friction, and it lands exactly when people are trying to enjoy a trip. Nimi was designed as a unified platform where groups manage trips, track expenses, and share memories in one place.

Problem statement

Fragmentation, not missing features.

Users struggle to access and manage information because data is distributed across multiple systems — producing fragmented workflows and increased cognitive load. Four issues surfaced repeatedly:

Information fragmentation

Users must navigate multiple systems to gather what they need, which slows workflows down.

Poor data visibility

Important insights stay hidden inside complex data structures.

Inefficient navigation

Time goes to searching for features instead of completing tasks.

Increased cognitive load

Interfaces carrying excessive information reduce usability and slow decisions.

Research & discovery

Who the product is actually for.

We analysed the platform's target population and demographic distribution to identify the primary user groups, behavioural patterns, and usability considerations that should drive design decisions.

01 · Core segment

The majority of users sit in the 25–30 band — digitally fluent people who value productivity-focused interfaces.

02 · Mobile-first

Users aged 19–30 access platforms through mobile or hybrid environments, making responsive design and simplified workflows essential.

03 · Secondary groups

Users 31+ interact more goal-oriented — they prefer clear navigation, predictable interfaces, minimal cognitive load.

04 · Accessibility

For the 40+ group, readable typography and clear hierarchy become an inclusivity requirement, not a preference.

Interview insights

Three scenarios that shaped the build.

Scenario 01

Shared photos, one safe place

Scenario

Capture and share photos on one platform with friends and family, through a secure medium.

Solution

Every member of a group can add photos to the photo pool for that particular trip memory.

Scenario 02

Multi-currency settlement

Scenario

Manage trip expenses when travelling across multiple countries and calculating in different currencies.

Solution

Users specify the settlement currency at the moment they add an expense.

Scenario 03

One app, not four

Scenario

Managing a journey across various applications is tense and often complex.

Solution

A unified experience: expense management, shared memories, photo gallery, and group chat together.

Personas

Two of the five, designed for first.

The segmentation board below surfaced five personalities that show up in almost every group trip. Two of them drove the build: the person who gets the trip organised, and the person who wants it to still mean something a year later. Everything in the product had to serve one of those two without getting in the other's way.

Group leader · Organiser · Type A

The Trip Planner

Herds the cats. Sets the trip up, pulls everyone in, and keeps the logistics moving while it's happening Goals
  • Everything about the trip in one place
  • Set up a trip and send invitations with minimal effort
  • Real-time organisation while the trip is underway, not after
  • Explain the premise of Nimi well enough that the group actually participates
Frustrations
  • Doing all the organising alone with no way to delegate
  • Chasing people for photos, money and confirmations across apps
  • Content arriving unstructured and needing to be sorted by hand
Design implication
  • Low-friction invite and link-sharing paths, permissions clear enough to hand off work, and expenses that settle without a spreadsheet
Natural storyteller · Likely souvenir customer

The Sentimental Archivist

The trip and the group carry high sentimental value. Wants more than the photos — wants the story Goals
  • Keep the story, beautifully, after the trip is over
  • More than a photo dump — memories with narrative and context
  • A single place holding everyone's pictures, not just their own
  • Something physical or lasting to come out of it
Frustrations
  • Camera rolls where the trip dissolves into thousands of loose images
  • Group chats that bury the good material within days
  • No way to relive the trip in order once everyone disperses
Design implication
  • Memories as narrative units rather than albums, per-trip cover images and colour themes, and a souvenir path that turns the trip into an object
Research artifact Audience segmentation Three axes we sorted users along, each answering a different prioritisation question.
Nimi usage behaviour Who do we prioritise when mapping new features?

How much effort a person will put into a trip once they're inside it.

Designer
  • Group leader / organiser / type A
  • Easy to set up a trip and send invitations
  • Help explaining the premise of Nimi and create motivations for the Group to participate
  • Easy tools to reorganise, restructure and design content to make a better Story
Contributor
  • Eager participants, mass photo takers, record-keepers
  • Easy to add photos and expenses
  • Lower the barrier to collaboration and co-designing
Resistor
  • Uninterested in Nimi's premise — key driver toward use is social pressure
  • Reminders that Nimi is happening (notifications)
  • Easy to "mass dump" content that others can structure
  • Nimi envy (amazing visual design)
Goal · product changes Move resistors → contributors and contributors → designers. The payoff of the finished trip is what does the work.
Comfort with mobile apps Who do we prioritise when making UX/UI decisions?

How much interface fluency we can assume — and who will actually re-use the app.

Technofile
  • Digital natives — Gen Z and Millennials (ages 10–40)
  • Ultra-familiar with digital experiences
  • Move quickly — expect to complete tasks in an app quickly
  • Expect engaging, dynamic content; video is a must to keep them interested
  • If it's not on social, it didn't happen
Digital-familiar
  • Older Millennials, Gen X, some Boomers (ages 35–75)
  • Use mobile apps for a specific purpose — social connection, quality of life
  • Barrier to download and use is high
  • Function and ease of use > visual stimulation
  • Need directly written cues to use the app
Technophobe
  • Reluctant smartphone users — typically older, Boomers and above
  • Unfamiliar with common UX/UI practices
  • Unlikely to download a "fun" mobile app
  • High emphasis on function, legibility and clear purpose
Personalities in the travel group Who do we prioritise in marketing efforts?

The five roles that show up in almost every group trip — each wanting a different thing from the same product.

Trip Planner
  • Group leader / organiser / type A
  • Herd the cats
  • Everything all in one place
  • Tool to make their job easier by allowing collaboration
  • Real-time organisation matters most (group chat solves this)
Sentimental Archivist
  • Natural storyteller
  • The trip and group have high sentimental value
  • Wants more than the photos — values the story as well
  • Likely souvenir customer
  • Easy to keep the story beautifully after the trip is over
Experience Enthusiast
  • "Master of fun" / social ringleader
  • Lives in the moment
  • Knows the destination and attractions, suggests activities — the Yelper
  • Framework for capturing the memories they inspire
"It's on me" big payer
  • Reaches for the wallet now, worries about settling up later
  • Big-ticket items to be divided up
  • Track expenses quickly and easily
  • Get paid back
Photo Hoarder
  • Not necessarily a photographer
  • Wants every. single. photo. from the trip
  • Often a parent or older family member
  • Single place for everyone's pictures
  • Easy to access and download at full quality
Goal · product changes Turn the experience enthusiast into an archivist — capture the trip they were already creating. Open question from the board: where do content creators fit?

Rebuilt as vector from the original research board. The three axes were deliberately kept separate: feature scope was argued from usage behaviour, interface decisions from app comfort, and positioning from group personality.

Research artifact Trip member types & permissions Five member states, the paths between them, and exactly what each one is allowed to do.

Scroll horizontally to follow the full state map →

Trip Creator
ENTRY · creates the trip
  • Can be added to memories and expenses
  • Can view all trip content and edit or create
  • Can make souvenirs
  • Can accept or ignore new trip members on a closed trip
  • Can delete trip members
  • Sets the countdown for capturing a trip
Trip Memberactive
ENTRY · invited, or accepted by creator
  • Can be added to memories and expenses
  • Can view all trip content and edit or create
  • Can make souvenirs
  • Can invite others and create ghost members
Pending Memberclosed trip only
ENTRY · invited, awaiting creator
  • Avatar visible only to themselves and the trip creator
  • Avatar is not editable
  • Cannot be added to memories or expenses
  • Cannot view any trip content beyond the pending screen
Inactive "Ghost" Membernot on Nimi
ENTRY · created by creator or a member
  • Can be added to memories and expenses
  • Not an active user, so cannot perform any function inside the trip
Merged Memberghost → active
ENTRY · claims an avatar when joining
  • Same permissions as a normal active trip member
  • Inherits everything the ghost was already tagged into
Non-trip Memberfuture · "wish you were here"
ENTRY · invited to view only
  • View all trip content and download images
  • Like memories, photos and comments
  • Cannot edit, add or change anything
  • Cannot make souvenirs

Rebuilt as vector from the original research board. Pinning permissions to a member state — rather than to a screen — is what made the invite, pending and group-settings flows tractable. The "ghost" member was the load-bearing idea: it let a group tag someone into memories and expenses before that person had ever installed Nimi.

For each of the five stages we tracked the action, the questions users raised, the friction that could break trust, and the moments that landed well. Registration length, chat privacy, and multi-currency confusion were the three recurring risks.

Cognitive cluster

Storyboard, Photo Pool and Gallery are one mental group — all three are places where trip content lives.

Cognitive cluster

Open tension

Rebuilt from the working board: two entry levels above eight destinations, each with the actions available inside it. The clusters mattered most — they are why Storyboard, Photo Pool and Gallery ended up adjacent in the N menu rather than in separate tabs.

Stage 03 Storyboards & journey wireframes Low-fidelity screens sequenced by flow — onboarding, new trip, invited, trip settings.
01Onboardingfirst launch → profileDone

Sign-in options through to nickname and avatar — the shortest possible path to a usable profile.

02New tripcreate → cover → publishOpen

The longest flow, and the only one still open: copy and tutorial videos outstanding, with a board note to surface the tutorial in the N menu.

03Invitedlink → claim → land in tripDone

Arriving from an invite link, claiming an avatar, and landing inside the trip rather than on a signup wall.

04Trip Settingsadding The GroupDone

Group management — adding people, editing profiles, and the toggle-styles exploration at the foot of the board.

The board split into its four flows, backgrounds removed so each sequence sits directly on the page. Statuses are as they stood on the board at handover.

Outcome

Where the research landed.

Three screens show how the research findings became product decisions — one shared home for the trip, one core gesture, and one legible answer to settling up.

Selected screens — the full flow is in the research above

Trip detailMemories, group and expenses in one view — one home for the trip instead of four apps.
N menuRadial quick-add: the single gesture that replaced hunting across tools.
Expense detailShares and settle-up made legible — the answer to "who owes whom?"

Impact & outcomes

What changed.

01 · Improved experience

Users navigate the platform more easily and complete tasks faster, through simplified navigation and better visual hierarchy.

02 · Faster task completion

Streamlined workflows and better-organised data reduced friction within the user journey.

03 · Reduced cognitive load

The original flows presented too much at once. Structured layouts, prioritised information, and contextual presentation replaced them.

04 · Better data visibility

Users identify trends and important information more easily, enabling faster decisions.

05 · Product scalability

The platform now supports additional features, new data sources, and future growth without compromising usability.
